About

A bit about me

I was born and raised in Seoul, and moving to the U.S. taught me that heritage isn’t something you leave behind — it’s a lens. Living between two cultures showed me how much of who we are is shaped by the society around us: language, family expectations, even what counts as success. It also showed me how immigrant families can fall through the gaps between two systems.

Research

Questions about people, health, and society

Real work — the social questions I've investigated, plus the scientific and technical skills I bring to them.

Sociology of HealthSocial DeterminantsStatistics

What really predicts life expectancy? Social conditions.

A UC Irvine COSMOS project — “Beyond the Human Development Index: How Socioeconomic Indicators Better Predict Life Expectancy.” We tested whether socioeconomic factors predict life expectancy better than common composite indices, and found (using linear models and forest plots) that healthcare spending acts indirectly rather than through a simple direct effect. The takeaway stuck with me: how long people live depends on the social and economic conditions around them — not just on how much a country spends on care.

Role: Co-author · presented as a research poster at the UC Irvine COSMOS symposium

ChemistryResearchPublication

Coating Drierite with methylene blue for oxygen indication

Published in the National High School Journal of Science (NHSJS). Commercial oxygen indicators usually need sensors and aren't cheap, so we coated Drierite — an inexpensive desiccant that already flags moisture — with colorless leucomethylene blue. In oxygen it oxidizes back to blue, so one low-cost material signals both moisture and oxygen (handy for glove boxes). We showed that spraying the coating beats soaking, which dissolves the Drierite, and tuned the reducing-agent chemistry to control the response time.

Role: Co-author (one of nine) · ran the spray-coating experiments, took the UV-Vis measurements, and compiled the data.
